publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Role of Site Shielding in Prediction Models for Urban Radiowave Propagation (Digest No. 1994/231)
IEE Colloquium on Role of Site Shielding in Prediction Models for Urban Radiowave Propagation (Digest No. 1994/231)
abstract: Microcellular coverage from a set of base stations on Southampton University campus is presented. The base station omnidirectional antennas were mounted below the urban sky-line, and measurements of received signal power and Rician K-factor distance profiles were made. Coverage plots for each microcell in terms of path loss enabled the shadowing effects of buildings and diffraction losses around corners to be quantified. Assigning channel sets to the base stations enabled the speculation of cluster sizes in urban environments to be made. A microcellular prediction tool provided predictions that were compared to the measured results.

articleTitle: Characterisation of building scatter of signals at microwave frequencies
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Role of Site Shielding in Prediction Models for Urban Radiowave Propagation (Digest No. 1994/231)
abstract: In assessing the effect of site shielding where multi-path interference is a distinct possibility, building, vegetation and terrain scatters are also important factors apart from diffraction around shielding obstacles. Particularly, building scatter has been long identified as a significant interference source in urban environments. In site shielding situations, distances from possibly scattering buildings are considerably limited by space in urban areas, typically in a range from a few hundred to a few thousand meters. At microwave frequencies, buildings are immensely large relatively to the wavelength. This means that distance is usually only a very small fraction of the Rayleigh far field distance, such as the order of one hundredth. The paper describes the development of a prediction model suitable to assess scattering behaviours of buildings in site shielding. The validity of this model has been examined against measurements made from a reflector and buildings at a frequency of 11.2 GHz.

articleTitle: Building scatter and vegetation attenuation measurements at 38 GHz
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Role of Site Shielding in Prediction Models for Urban Radiowave Propagation (Digest No. 1994/231)
abstract: Several measurements have been made to determine the extent of scatter and attenuation of 38 GHz line of sight links by buildings and vegetation. Measured co- and cross-polar reflection profiles of a typical brick building are presented. A profile of incoming signal was measured for a receive antenna in a cluttered building environment, the results of which are compared with the field predicted by the ray-tracing model, currently under development at RAL. Measurements were made of the field propagated through vegetation at various receive heights such that the effects of foliage and tree trunks could be studied. Results are presented in several forms, including plots of attenuation versus vegetation depth, giving a value of the attenuation per metre for the tree type present.

articleTitle: Preliminary results from a bistatic Doppler radar operating at 42 GHz
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Role of Site Shielding in Prediction Models for Urban Radiowave Propagation (Digest No. 1994/231)
abstract: A state of the art coherent carrier wave 41.5 GHz bistatic radar has been used to observe rainfall, snow and fog scatter together with Doppler spread over a period of approximately three months. These data indicate the significance of rainfall scatter at millimetre frequencies and the radar proves itself as a very sensitive tool for the detection of wind shear in the presence of precipitation.

articleTitle: Experimental study on the variability of site shielding factor on trans-horizon radio link
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Role of Site Shielding in Prediction Models for Urban Radiowave Propagation (Digest No. 1994/231)
abstract: One very effective method of reducing interfering signal levels is to shield the receiving antenna from the interfering source using an obstacle, e.g. a building. For non-uniformly distributed fields a problem arises in determining the shielding effectiveness of an obstacle. In the line-of-sight case, the signal level received in the radio shadow can be determined by using diffraction theory techniques. The shielding of the obstacle can be described by the diffraction loss. A 50 km link, operating at 11.2 GHz, has been established over the Bristol Channel in the United Kingdom. The initial results from monitoring the signal level on the radio link for 12 consecutive months are discussed.

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Role of Site Shielding in Prediction Models for Urban Radiowave Propagation (Digest No. 1994/231)
abstract: A non line of sight 42 GHz point to point link has been set up specifically to measure and study the anomalous propagation activity at 42 GHz across an estuary and marsh land in Essex. The link was originally set up under direct line of sight conditions (the antennas are narrow beam width) and the receiver was then moved down to a much lower height and a non line of sight path. Preliminary results and analysis indicate that anomalous propagation certainly does exist at 42 GHz, Transmissions can be bent over non line of sight paths. The authors have recorded anomalous radio refractive index induced activity over significant periods of time. Over much shorter periods rainfall scatter has been observed to produce over the horizon propagation.

articleTitle: Measurement of reflections from building surfaces
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Role of Site Shielding in Prediction Models for Urban Radiowave Propagation (Digest No. 1994/231)
abstract: Future propagation planning will rely heavily on the exact specification of building parameters. However, building parameters which have a significant effect on propagation have not currently been identified. Therefore a program to measure the type of reflections from building walls has been undertaken. Several wall structures have been measured in order to determine the specular reflection and scattering which may occur. The aim is to identify the significance of the construction and materials used to build the walls. The paper describes the method used to perform the measurements and presents the results.
